title: The Rewind: Global Financial Crisis
summary:
Risk aversion, fear of loss is the element that keeps markets
safe and sane. And when risk aversion evaporates, unwise deals can be done and people take on too
much risk. And when they take on too much risk, it's invariably followed by a period
in which risk bearing is punished, not rewarded.

reader_summary.headline: Today, we're featuring another episode of The Rewind.
reader_summary.overview: Today, we're featuring another episode of The Rewind, in which Howard looks back on some of his memos over the years, discusses their origins. In this episode, Howard reflects on memos related to the global financial crisis with Bob O'Leary, the co-portfolio manager for Oak Tree's Global Opportunities Strategy. Howard and Bob were interviewed by Anna Schumansky, Oak Tree's senior financial writer.

thesis: The speakers argue that the years 2005 to 2007 featured a period of overly positive market psychology and risk aversion evaporating, which led investors to engage in a search for returns through unwise deals and excessive risk-taking. They contend that this environment, characterized by an escalating auction for capital where lenders competed to accept the lowest returns and weakest documents, inevitably resulted in a period where risk-bearing was punished rather than rewarded.
